title: Why stars twinkle but planets shine steadily
group: HOWN — How and Why in Nature
examples: How can I tell a planet from a star?

explain.say: Starlight crosses space for years, then in the last moment passes through Earth's air. The air is full of drifting pockets of warm and cool air that bend light by slightly different amounts.

explain.say: Stars are so far away that each one is just a tiny point of light, a single thin beam. As air pockets drift past, that beam is bent this way and that, so the star seems to flicker and shift.

explain.say: Planets are much closer, so through a telescope they look like little discs. Light from each part of the disc is jiggled differently, and the wobbles cancel out, so a planet shines with a steady glow.

explain.say: Stars twinkle most near the horizon, where their light passes through more air. That gives a handy rule: if a bright dot in the night sky isn't twinkling, it is probably a planet.

faq.a: Their light passes through moving layers of warm and cool air, which bend it slightly differently from moment to moment. Because a star is just a tiny point, these wobbles make it flicker. Astronomers call it scintillation.
Planets are close enough to appear as tiny discs rather than points. Each bit of the disc twinkles separately, and the flickers average out, so the planet looks steady.
asks: How can I tell a planet from a star?

faq.a: No. Above the atmosphere there is no moving air to bend the light, so astronauts and space telescopes see stars as steady points.
asks: Would stars twinkle on the Moon?

faq.q: Why do stars twinkle more near the horizon?
faq.a: Near the horizon, starlight travels through much more air before it reaches you, so there are more moving pockets to bend it. Low bright stars can even flash red and green.
asks: Why do low stars flash colours?

faq.a: Twinkling blurs fine detail in telescope pictures. That's why big telescopes are built on high, dry mountains, use mirrors that bend to cancel the wobble, or go into space like the Hubble Space Telescope.
asks: Why are telescopes put in space?

facts: The Hubble Space Telescope, launched in 1990, orbits above the atmosphere, so stars don't twinkle in its images.

quiz.say: A bright dot in the evening sky shines without twinkling at all. What is it most likely to be?
quiz.show: A bright dot that doesn't twinkle is most likely…
quiz.why: Planets look like tiny discs, so the air's wobbles average out and they shine steadily.

wrong.1: Stars are single points, so they twinkle, especially near the horizon.
wrong.2: A shooting star streaks across the sky in a second; it doesn't stay put.
